text.headline: Walkability in Los Angeles
text.text: A timeline of planning decisions, environmental burdens, and research milestones that explain why walkability is uneven across LA County.

text.headline: Early zoning begins to structure opportunity
text.text:
Los Angeles starts using land-use regulation in ways the city's Historical Housing and Land Use Study later ties to racialized separation of housing, industry, and neighborhood investment.

Historical Housing and Land Use Study

text.headline: The Arroyo Seco Parkway opens
text.text:
LADOT's transportation history identifies the Arroyo Seco Parkway as the nation's first freeway. It marks the region's decisive turn toward auto-oriented mobility and corridor building.

Transportation Topics and Tales

text.headline: Los Angeles' original zoning code takes effect
text.text:
The city's original zoning code goes into effect and helps lock land-use patterns into formal policy. Those rules continue to influence where housing, jobs, and mobility options concentrate.

Historical Housing and Land Use Study

text.headline: Walking to school in inner-city Los Angeles centers safety
text.text:
Banerjee and coauthors show that children's walking experience in inner-city Los Angeles is shaped by traffic danger, crime, and neighborhood disorder, not just sidewalk presence.

Banerjee et al. (2014)

text.headline: LA trip-making studies link walkability to fewer car trips
text.text:
Research on Los Angeles travel behavior finds that neighborhood walkability changes trip generation and trip chaining, tying local street form to regional vehicle dependence.

Lee (2015)

text.headline: Socioeconomic context changes what walkability means
text.text:
Adkins and colleagues argue that relationships between built environments and walking vary by socioeconomic context, so the same street features do not produce the same mobility outcomes everywhere.

Adkins et al. (2017)

text.headline: Safe routes to parks become an environmental justice question
text.text:
Rigolon and coauthors examine who has more walkable routes to parks in Los Angeles, showing that access to recreation depends on both neighborhood design and unequal exposure to street hazards.

Rigolon et al. (2018)

text.headline: Heat research reframes walkability as climate exposure
text.text:
Southern California temperature research shows that vegetation and land cover matter for street-level heat, strengthening the link between walkability, shade, and climate resilience.

Engel et al. (2022) and Vahmani and Ban-Weiss (2016)

text.headline: Micro-level features explain walkability inequity in Los Angeles
text.text:
Ki and Chen show that overlooked street-scale features help explain why headline walkability measures can miss inequity within Los Angeles neighborhoods.

Ki and Chen (2023)

text.headline: Asthma evidence ties built form to public health in LA
text.text:
The Los Angeles asthma case study links built-environment conditions to asthma outcomes, pushing walkability analysis beyond mobility into neighborhood health risk.

Kim et al. (2023)

text.headline: Behavioral data exposes the mismatch between walkability and walking
text.text:
Mobile phone traces and street-view imagery show that walkability scores and actual walking behavior do not always align, opening the door to more behavior-aware measurement.

He and He (2024)

text.headline: Next-generation walkability metrics move to perception and AI
text.text:
New work on perceived walkability and multimodal AI argues that future walkability measures should capture what people actually see, feel, and do at street level, not only what coarse GIS variables can approximate.

Ki et al. (2025) and Van Der Vlugt et al. (2025)
